phonemes.desc: Unstressed open [ma], the light first syllable — the 'ma' of 'matter' held brief.
Voiceless dental fricative [θ], the 'th' of English 'thin' — Welsh writes it with the digraph th, sharply distinct from dd, which is the voiced 'th' of 'this'.
Short stressed [ɔ], the 'o' of 'off', carrying the word's penultimate stress, as Welsh words do.
Welsh w is a full vowel, here short [ʊ] like the 'u' of 'put'; ch is the voiceless velar fricative [x], the rough ch of Scottish 'loch'.

pronunciation.approximation: ma-THOL-ukh — stress the middle syllable; 'th' as in 'thin'; the w is a short 'oo'-like vowel; the final ch is the rough, breathy ch of Scottish 'loch', as in modern Welsh.

pronunciation.note: Matholwch is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Middle Welsh form is already plain ASCII — Welsh writes its distinctive sounds with Latin digraphs (th, ch) and the vowel-letter w, none of which carries a diacritic or a letter the ASCII alphabet lacks. The capital alone distinguishes the temple form from the input; the king's standing in the tale is beside the point.

domains.title: The King Across the Sea
domains.subtitle: The Thirteen Ships, the Maimed Horses, and the Cauldron of Rebirth
domains.lead: Matholwch is the king of Ireland in the Second Branch of the Mabinogi, Branwen ferch Llŷr: the bridegroom who came with thirteen ships to Harlech to ask for Branwen's hand, the wronged man appeased with gold and a cauldron that raises the dead, and the husband who could not shield his queen when the insult of the maimed horses came home to his court — the man whose marriage laid two islands waste.

cards.name: The Thirteen Ships
cards.desc: The fleet that brought him to Harlech to ask for Branwen — Ireland arriving as a suitor, and sailing home as a husband.

cards.name: The Maimed Horses
cards.desc: Efnisien's insult — lips, ears, tails, and eyelids cut to the bone — the wound no compensation could make Ireland forget.

cards.name: The Cauldron of Rebirth
cards.desc: Given to Matholwch in recompense: the slain cast in at evening rise fighting-fit by morning — all but their speech.

cards.name: The Starling
cards.desc: Branwen's tamed messenger, taught to speak, carrying her letter across the sea to Brân when no ship could sail.

symbols.name: The thirteen ships
symbols.meaning: Sea-borne kingship — the power that comes across the water to ask, and can always sail away

symbols.name: The maimed horses
symbols.meaning: An insult done to property but felt in honor — the wound that recompense could not close

symbols.name: The Cauldron of Rebirth
symbols.meaning: Resurrection without speech: the body restored, the voice withheld

symbols.name: The starling
symbols.meaning: The smallest thing in the tale that crosses the sea — a tamed bird against a kingdom's embargo

symbols.name: The house of a hundred pillars
symbols.meaning: Peace built as a trap: a pillar for every beam, a bag on every pillar, an armed man in every bag

mythology.lead: Matholwch has essentially one story — but it is the Second Branch of the Mabinogi, Branwen ferch Llŷr, the tale medieval Welsh literature remembers as its national tragedy: a marriage between the two islands that ends with the hosts of both destroyed.

myths.title: The Thirteen Ships at Harlech
myths.text: Bendigeidfran — Brân the Blessed, crowned king of Britain — was seated on the rock of Harlech above the sea, with his brother Manawydan and his half-brothers Nisien and Efnisien, when they saw thirteen ships coming from the south of Ireland, fair and swift, their shields above their gunwales. It was Matholwch, king of Ireland, come to ask for Branwen, Brân's sister, fairest maiden in the world, so that Ireland and the Island of the Mighty might be joined by marriage and grow stronger together. Brân consented, and the wedding was held at Aberffraw — and because no house had ever been built that could contain Brân, they slept in tents.

myths.title: The Maiming of the Horses
myths.text:
Efnisien, the half-brother whose gift was quarreling, had not been consulted, and he took the omission as an insult to his honor. Coming on Matholwch's horses stabled apart, he asked whose they were, and hearing, he fell on them in a rage: he cut their lips back to the teeth, their ears back to their heads, their tails to the skin, and their eyelids back to the bone. Matholwch's men could make no sense of it — a king given a bride and mutilated horses in the same week. They armed for home in silence, which Brân read rightly as the beginning of a war.

Brân sent an embassy led by Manawydan to ask what recompense would content him. Matholwch was offered the full replacement of the horses, a silver staff as tall as himself, a golden platter as broad as his face — and, beyond all price, the Cauldron of Rebirth. The tale is exact about the transaction: the honor-price was paid, the peace was sworn, and neither was ever real again.

myths.title: The Cauldron of Rebirth
myths.text:
Matholwch asked where such a cauldron had come from, and Brân told him: it had come to him out of Ireland itself. A man named Llassar Llaes Gyfnewid and his wife Cymidei Cymeinfoll — a woman who gave birth to a fully armed warrior every six weeks — had fled the Irish king's plot to burn them alive in a white-hot iron house, and had brought the cauldron with them to Wales. Its property was this: cast a slain warrior into it at evening, and by morning he rises as fighting-fit as before, except that he never again has the power of speech.

So the cauldron returned to Ireland as a wedding-gift of reconciliation — a thing that cancels death but keeps its silence, given to heal an insult that would not stay healed. The irony is the tale's own: the Irish fought their last battle with it, feeding their slain back into the war, until it was destroyed from within.

myths.title: The Starling and the Crossing of the Sea
myths.text:
Matholwch sailed home with his bride, and Ireland welcomed her; gifts were given, and in due time she bore a son, Gwern. But the insult of the horses would not lie down. Matholwch's nobles nursed the grudge until they drove their king to atone for it: Branwen was put out of the chamber and into the kitchen, and the butcher came every day and struck her a blow on the ear. All passage to Wales was stopped, so that no word could reach her brother.

Branwen reared a starling at the edge of the kneading-trough, taught it speech, tied her letter beneath its wing, and sent it across the sea. The bird found Brân at Caer Seint in Arfon and settled on his shoulder. What followed is the great set-piece of the branch: the crowned king of Britain crossed the sea at the head of his host — wading, for no ship could hold him — and when the Irish destroyed the bridges and his men asked his counsel, he answered with the sentence Welsh has never let go: 'A fo ben, bid bont' — he who would be a leader, let him be a bridge — and lay down across the river so the host could pass over him.

myths.title: The Hundred Pillars and the End of the Cauldron
myths.text:
The Irish sued for peace on their knees: they would give the kingship of Ireland to Gwern, Matholwch's son by Branwen, and build Brân a house — the first ever made that could hold him. The house was raised with a hundred pillars, and on every pillar a bag, and in every bag an armed man. Efnisien came in first to inspect the peace, asked what was in the bags — 'Flour,' they said — and crushed each head between his fingers, one by one, until he felt the bone give.

At the feast the boy Gwern was passed lovingly from lap to lap until he came to Efnisien's, and Efnisien rose and cast him into the fire. Branwen would have leapt after her son; Brân held her with one hand and took up his shield with the other. Then came the battle the whole tale had been marching toward. The Irish threw their slain into the Cauldron of Rebirth and sent them back each morning, mute and fighting — until Efnisien, in the act that pays for all the rest, lay down among the Irish dead as if slain, was cast into the cauldron with the corpses, and stretched himself out inside it until the cauldron burst in pieces and his own heart burst with it. Of the Irish there escaped only five pregnant women, from whom the five provinces of Ireland were repeopled; of the Welsh host, seven men — Pryderi, Manawydan, Glifieu, Taliesin, Ynawg, Grudyeu, and Heilyn — and Brân, dying of a poisoned spear in the foot, who bade them cut off his head and carry it home. Branwen died of a broken heart on the bank of the Alaw, crying that two good islands had been laid waste because of her. Of Matholwch himself the tale says nothing more: he is not given a death-scene, only swallowed in the general ruin of his kingdom.

lore.syncretism: Matholwch is a Welsh invention wearing an Irish crown, and the tradition knows it: no Irish-language tale names him, and his kingship of Ireland exists only inside Branwen ferch Llŷr. The honest comparisons are structural, and Proinsias Mac Cana's monograph Branwen Daughter of Llŷr mapped them: Brân's sea-crossing against the Voyage of Bran mac Febail (Immram Brain), the children of Llŷr against the Irish family of Lir, and above all the Cauldron of Rebirth against the cauldron-lore of Ireland — the Dagda's cauldron from Murias, from which no company went away unsatisfied, is the standard parallel for the Celtic vessel of inexhaustible power. The Welsh and Irish cauldrons divide the two ends of the motif between them: Ireland's feeds the living, Wales's revives the dead — and takes their speech as payment. Arthurian scholarship, from Loomis onward, has long set the cauldron and the carried head beside the Grail procession of Peredur; the comparison is illuminating and unprovable, and this temple registers it as such.
lore.culturalLegacy: Matholwch entered the world's reading with Lady Charlotte Guest's translation of the Mabinogion (1838–49), which carried the Second Branch into English and made the maimed horses and the Cauldron of Rebirth part of the general inheritance of fantasy literature. Ifor Williams's Pedeir Keinc y Mabinogi (1930) fixed the text for scholarship, and Sioned Davies's translation (2007) is the modern English standard. The branch's sentences have never left Welsh letters — 'a fo ben, bid bont' is quoted wherever leadership is discussed — and Evangeline Walton's The Children of Llyr (1971) retells the whole catastrophe as a novel. The cauldron motif, transmitting through the Welsh tradition, stands behind every modern cauldron that raises armies of the dead; Lloyd Alexander's Prydain chronicles drew freely on the Mabinogion's world. On Anglesey, the Bronze Age cairn beside the river Alaw still answers to the name Bedd Branwen, Branwen's grave — the tale's one fixed point in the landscape of two islands.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Matholwch is the king who accepted the compensation and could not accept it. Nothing in the tale is more carefully drawn than the failure of the settlement: the horses replaced, the silver staff, the golden platter, the cauldron itself — a full honor-price, formally paid, formally received. And still the insult kept working, not in him alone but in his nobles, until it expelled the queen to the kitchen and the butcher's daily blow. The Second Branch is the Mabinogion's treatise on the difference between settling a wrong and healing one.

His cauldron is the perfect emblem of the settlement's logic: it undoes the death and keeps the silence. The men who climb out of it fight as well as ever and cannot speak — cannot say what the war cost, cannot forgive, cannot testify. Matholwch ends as he began, a king whose kingdom is decided by what others do around him: Efnisien maims his horses, his nobles disgrace his wife, his guests massacre his peace, his bridegroom's gift arms his own destruction. The tale does not even grant him a death. It grants him something more instructive — a marriage made in good faith between two islands, and the proof that good faith is not enough when honor has been taught to count higher.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Middle Welsh form is Matholwch — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. Middle Welsh was written in the Latin alphabet, and its distinctive sounds are carried by digraphs (th, ch, ll) and the vowel-letter w, none of which the ASCII set lacks. The earlier monumental scripts of the two islands — the ogham stones of Ireland and Wales — predate the manuscript tradition, but no attestation of this name has ever been read on any of them. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: matholwch.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Matholwch is a textual figure: no inscription, ogham stone, or place-name in Ireland names him, and his kingship exists entirely within the Welsh tale. His manuscript witnesses are exact — the Second Branch survives complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, National Library of Wales, Peniarth MS 4, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1375–1425), the two great codices on which Williams's edition rests. The tale's one fixed point in the landscape is Welsh: Bedd Branwen, the cairn beside the river Alaw on Anglesey where the branch says Branwen was buried, is a genuine Bronze Age burial monument — cremation urns were recovered when the cairn was opened in the early nineteenth century, and later excavations confirmed its prehistoric date. The name attached to it is medieval folklore, not prehistory — but it proves the story was already rooted in Welsh ground centuries ago. The nearest epigraphic kin of his name-element are the Gaulish personal names in Matu- (Matugenos and kin): comparative evidence only, never identification.
